newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Eurobourses down despite BT deal, dlr drifts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Eurobourses down despite BT deal, dlr drifts.

text.p: European bourses were weaker on Monday morning, with London a few points down despite a jump in British Telecom shares after the surprise weekend news of its planned $20 billion merger with America's MCI Communications.
On the currency markets, dealers said the dollar was drifting and would struggle to make any gains ahead of Tuesday's U.S. presidential elections.
By 1000 GMT BT shares had climbed 29p to 380p but the blue chip FTSE 100 index was down 2.0 points at 3,947.2.

London trading continued the subdued tone of last week with business cautious ahead of the U.S. elections and as domestic political worries revived after the death at the weekend of a Conservative MP reduced the ruling party's majority to one. No major companies were reporting on Monday and corporate news was thin on the ground.

The FTSE 100 closed last week at its lowest level for a month and dealers said the market remained pre-occupied over further interest rate rises after last week's unanticipated quarter percentage point tightening of monetary policy.
"The rise in UK rates last week has changed the tide of stock market sentiment in front of the budget (next week)" one trader said.

In Frankfurt German shares were half a percent down in floor trading and dealers said the market was catching up with profit-taking during late Friday's electronic dealings. The 30-share DAX index was down 16.18 points at 2,667.15.

In Paris too the mood was negative and French shares started with modest losses, shadowing a downward drift in bond markets. Traders said operators were marking time ahead of the U.S. poll and little action was expected.
Meanwhile, the dollar drifted, edging marginally lower, and analysts said it would struggle to make gains ahead of U.S. election results.

The re-election of President Bill Clinton was seen as a foregone conclusion, but the market feared the Democrats could wrest control of Congress from the Republicans and loosen trade and fiscal policy.

"The market's cautious ahead of the elections and there are lingering fears the Democrats are going to get a clean sweep -- though I think those fears are overdone," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London.
Trading was further subdued overnight by a Japanese holiday.
Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank, said market jitters over the outcome of the U.S. vote meant the immediate risks for the dollar were to the downside.
"Concerns remain that in the event of a Democrat clean sweep protectionist influences will come back to the fore," he said.
Last Friday's comments by former U.S. treasury secretary Lloyd Bentsen highlighted that risk, Fox said.

Bentsen told Reuters Financial Television he was comfortable with the dollar's current exchange rate but would prefer not to see dollar/yen rise further. Substantial appreciation from here would put the U.S. at a competitive disadvantage, he said.
CURRENCIES AT 1000 GMT
The dollar was trading at 1.5132 marks and 113.16 yen compared with late Friday's 1.5183 marks and 113.40 yen. STOCKS MARKETS AT 1000 GMT London's FTSE 100 index was down 2.0 points at 3947.2
The Paris CAC-40 index was down 2.32 at 2138.19.
The Frankfurt DAX index was down 16.18 at 2667.15.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was firmer in early Europe at $378.60, compared with 377.65 at the London close on Friday. Silver was at $4.82.
